lines: A blank 3HP panel carrying the Mockba Modular logo, for filling a gap in the rack
Menu — Background theme repaints every Mockba Modular module in the rack Light, Dark or Aged, and that choice becomes the default for new ones
A 3HP attenuator that passes one signal through at the level set, with a VCA input for controlling that level from the patch
Scales the signal from silence at one end of its travel to full at the other; with nothing patched to input the module puts out a steady voltage instead, 0V to 10V across the same travel
The voltage here divided by 10 multiplies the level, so 10V passes the signal at the level the knob sets and 0V silences it
The signal to be attenuated
The attenuated signal
Menu — Exponential gives the level knob a logarithmic taper, so the lower part of its travel changes the level more slowly
A 3HP stereo attenuator that passes a left and a right signal through at the level set, with a VCA input for controlling that level from the patch
Scales both signals from silence at one end of its travel to full at the other
The voltage here divided by 10 multiplies the level, so 10V passes the signals at the level the knob sets and 0V silences them
The left signal to be attenuated
The right signal to be attenuated
The attenuated left signal
The attenuated right signal
Menu — Exponential gives the level knob a logarithmic taper, so the lower part of its travel changes the level more slowly
A 3HP multimode filter of the Moog ladder kind, with low pass, high pass and band pass responses
A three-position switch choosing the response: low pass, high pass or band pass
Sets the cutoff frequency, from about 20Hz at 0% to about 20kHz at 100%
The voltage here divided by 10 scales the cutoff setting, 10V leaving the cutoff where the knob puts it and 0V dropping it to about 8Hz
Adds resonance around the cutoff, from none at one end of its travel to close to self-oscillation at the other
The voltage here divided by 10 scales the resonance set by reso, 10V leaving it where the knob puts it and 0V removing it
Trims the level of the filtered signal, -25dB to +25dB, with no change at the centre
The signal to be filtered
The filtered signal
A 3HP crossfader between two signals, with a VCA input and a phase switch on the second one
Crossfades between the two inputs, input a alone at one end of its travel and input b alone at the other
A voltage of -5V to +5V here takes over from the a<->b knob, -5V giving input a alone and +5V input b alone
The voltage here divided by 10 multiplies the mixed signal, so 10V passes it at full level and 0V silences it
One of the two signals crossfaded
The other of the two signals crossfaded
A switch that flips the sign of input b before the crossfade, reading Normal in one position and Inverted in the other
The crossfade of the two inputs; with nothing patched to input a it carries a steady voltage instead, -5V to +5V across the travel of the a<->b knob
A 3HP mixer summing three signals, each with its own level knob
Sets the level of the signal at input a, following the square of the knob position
The first of the three signals summed
Sets the level of the signal at input b, following the square of the knob position
The second of the three signals summed
Sets the level of the signal at input c, following the square of the knob position
The third of the three signals summed
The three inputs summed; the sum is divided by the three gains added together, so the level stays roughly steady as more channels are opened
Menu — Additive Mix drops that division, so the three signals are summed as they are and the level rises with each one added
A 3HP clock divider with five gate outputs, each running at half the rate of the one before; it counts downwards so that all five start together
Each rise past 1V steps the divider on
A rise past 1V returns the divider to its starting state
10V for one clock and 0V for the next, so half the clock rate
10V for two clocks and 0V for two, so a quarter of the clock rate
10V for four clocks and 0V for four, so an eighth of the clock rate
10V for eight clocks and 0V for eight, so a sixteenth of the clock rate
10V for sixteen clocks and 0V for sixteen, so a thirty-second of the clock rate
A 3HP binary counter that counts clock pulses upwards and puts the five lowest bits of the count out as gates
Each rise past 1V adds one to the count
A rise past 1V sets the count back to zero
10V for one clock and 0V for the next, so half the clock rate
10V for two clocks and 0V for two, so a quarter of the clock rate
10V for four clocks and 0V for four, so an eighth of the clock rate
10V for eight clocks and 0V for eight, so a sixteenth of the clock rate
10V for sixteen clocks and 0V for sixteen, so a thirty-second of the clock rate
A 3HP selector passing one of four inputs through to a single output
A four-position switch choosing which input reaches output: a, b, c or d
A voltage here takes over from the select switch: below 2.5V chooses input a, below 5V input b, below 7.5V input c, and 7.5V or more input d
One of the four signals, carried to output while it is the one selected
Carries whichever of the four inputs is selected
A 3HP ADSR envelope generator
Sets how long the envelope takes to rise to its peak, 1ms at one end of its travel and 10 seconds at the other
Sets how long the envelope takes to fall from the peak to the sustain level, 1ms at one end of its travel and 10 seconds at the other
Sets the level held while the gate stays up, 0% to 100% of the full 10V
Sets how long the envelope takes to fall back to 0V after the gate drops, 1ms at one end of its travel and 10 seconds at the other
The envelope rises while the voltage here is 1V or more and falls once it drops below that
A rise here starts the attack again without the gate having to drop first
The envelope, 0V to 10V
Two sample and hold sections in 3HP, each capturing a voltage when it is triggered and holding it until the next trigger
A rise above 0V captures the voltage at that section's input
The voltage captured by that section when it is triggered; with this jack empty the section captures a random voltage instead, drawn from a normal distribution with a standard deviation of 2.5V
Holds the voltage that section captured at its last trigger
A 3HP panner, splitting one signal between a left and a right output
Sets the position between the two outputs, everything to L out at one end of its travel and everything to R out at the other
A voltage of -5V to +5V here takes over from the pan knob, -5V putting everything to L out and +5V everything to R out
The signal to be panned
The left share of the signal
The right share of the signal
Menu — Constant Power pans on a sine and cosine law rather than a straight one, which keeps the loudness even across the sweep
A 3HP range adapter, mapping an incoming span of voltage onto a different outgoing one
The input voltage that comes out as O/min, -10V to +10V
The input voltage that comes out as O/max, -10V to +10V
The voltage to be remapped
The voltage put out when the input is at I/min, -10V to +10V
The voltage put out when the input is at I/max, -10V to +10V
The remapped voltage, clamped to -12V to +12V
A 3HP phase distortion oscillator of the Casio CZ kind, putting out a saw wave, and switchable down to LFO speeds
Switches the oscillator into its low frequency range and turns the fine knob into a steady offset added to the output, -5V to +5V
Sets the pitch in semitones, 0 giving C4 at 261.63Hz and reaching 54 semitones either side of that
Detunes the pitch by up to three semitones either way; with lfo switched on it sets the offset added to the output instead, -5V to +5V
Added to the pitch, a volt per octave
Sets how far the wave is distorted, from the plain shape at one end of its travel to the fully distorted one at the other; with the shape mod jack patched it attenuates that voltage instead
The voltage here divided by 10, scaled by the shape knob, sets how far the wave is distorted
The oscillator's wave, -5V to +5V

A 3HP comparator, putting the result of comparing two voltages out on four gates
One of the two voltages compared; an empty jack counts as 0V
10V while the voltage at input a is below the voltage at input b, 0V otherwise
10V while the two voltages are exactly equal, 0V otherwise
10V while the two voltages differ, 0V otherwise
10V while the voltage at input a is above the voltage at input b, 0V otherwise
Three logic buffers in 3HP, each turning its input into a clean gate
A voltage above 1V here counts as true; an empty jack counts as false
10V while that buffer's input counts as true, 0V otherwise
Three inverters in 3HP, working either on logic gates or on the signal itself
A two-position switch choosing Digital, where each section inverts a gate, or Analog, where each section flips the sign of the voltage at its input
In Digital the voltage here counts as true above 1V, an empty jack counting as false; in Analog it is the signal whose sign is flipped
In Digital, 10V while that section's input is false and 0V while it is true; in Analog, that section's input with its sign flipped
Two OR gates in 3HP, each with two inputs
One of the two inputs of that gate; a voltage above 1V counts as true and an empty jack counts as false
10V while at least one of that gate's two inputs is true, 0V otherwise
Two NOR gates in 3HP, each with two inputs
One of the two inputs of that gate; a voltage above 1V counts as true and an empty jack counts as false
10V only while both of that gate's inputs are false, 0V otherwise
Two AND gates in 3HP, each with two inputs
One of the two inputs of that gate; a voltage above 1V counts as true and an empty jack counts as false
10V only while both of that gate's inputs are true, 0V otherwise
Two NAND gates in 3HP, each with two inputs
One of the two inputs of that gate; a voltage above 1V counts as true and an empty jack counts as false
0V only while both of that gate's inputs are true, 10V otherwise
Two XOR gates in 3HP, each with two inputs
One of the two inputs of that gate; a voltage above 1V counts as true and an empty jack counts as false
10V while exactly one of that gate's two inputs is true, 0V otherwise
Two XNOR gates in 3HP, each with two inputs
One of the two inputs of that gate; a voltage above 1V counts as true and an empty jack counts as false
10V while that gate's two inputs are both true or both false, 0V otherwise
A 3HP priority selector: its output goes high when high is true, or when low and raise are both true
A voltage above 1V counts as true; with raise also true it takes output to 10V
A voltage above 1V counts as true; with low also true it takes output to 10V
A voltage above 1V counts as true, and takes output to 10V on its own
10V while high is true, or while low and raise are both true; 0V otherwise
Named Mastah on the panel: it broadcasts the clock and reset it is given over the network, as UDP messages on port 7000, so that copies of Rack on other computers can run to the same clock
Each rise above 0V broadcasts a clock message
Each rise above 0V broadcasts a reset message
Note — the lamp lights red if the network socket cannot be opened or a message cannot be sent
Note — messages go to 192.168.1.255 unless a different address is written into MockbaModular.json in Rack's user folder; wired networking carries them more reliably than wireless
Named Slavah on the panel: it receives the clock and reset that Mastah broadcasts, as UDP messages on port 7000, and turns them back into pulses; one of these runs on each computer being synchronised
Closes and reopens the network socket, and sends a pulse from reset
A 1ms 10V pulse for each clock message received
A 1ms 10V pulse for each reset message received
Note — the lamp lights red if the network socket cannot be opened
